title: The big pack can cost more
hook: A larger pack looks like a bargain. What happens per kilogram?

knows: that a model can declare hypothetical quantities
doesNotKnow: Normalize different pack masses to cost per kilogram.

misconception: The largest pack always has the lowest unit price.
objective: Normalize different pack masses to cost per kilogram.

claims.text: A costs €3 for 500g. B costs €6 for 900g. Scaled model; prices fictional; same product.
claims.source: Declared hypothetical inputs and limits in resource-specs.json. No actual product, price, tariff, shelf-life, treatment or physical appliance specification is asserted.

claims.text: The stage's two results are computed by the printed expressions. At Large-price=6€, A=6€/kg and B=6.667€/kg. The geometry pictures follow the declared dimension relationships; other stage pictures are scaled to the larger displayed comparison and icons are not literal item counts.
claims.source: src/lib/lifehacks/resource-specs.json contains this lesson's numeric AST; src/lib/lifehacks/resource-model.ts evaluates it. A=["/",3,0.5]; B=["/","x",0.9]; x denotes Large-price. At x=6, A=6, B=6.66666666667; recall at x=7.5: B=8.33333333333. Values are fictional/ideal assumptions, not measurements. Display rounds to at most three decimals.

claims.text: Dividing price by kilograms puts both packs on the same denominator. Pack size alone does not determine unit price; the receipt and quantity must travel together.
claims.source: src/lib/lifehacks/resource-specs.json contains this lesson's numeric AST; src/lib/lifehacks/resource-model.ts evaluates it. A=["/",3,0.5]; B=["/","x",0.9]; x denotes Large-price. At x=6, A=6, B=6.66666666667; recall at x=7.5: B=8.33333333333. Values are fictional/ideal assumptions, not measurements. Display rounds to at most three decimals. The principle follows from those expressions and stated scenario limits.

claims.text: A costs €3 for 500g. B costs €6 for 900g. Change only Large-price to 7.5€. What is B (900g) now? Correct: 8.333€/kg. Use B's stated rule with Large-price=7.5€: it gives 8.333€/kg. Dividing price by kilograms puts both packs on the same denominator. Pack size alone does not determine unit price; the receipt and quantity must travel together.
claims.source: src/lib/lifehacks/resource-specs.json contains this lesson's numeric AST; src/lib/lifehacks/resource-model.ts evaluates it. A=["/",3,0.5]; B=["/","x",0.9]; x denotes Large-price. At x=6, A=6, B=6.66666666667; recall at x=7.5: B=8.33333333333. Values are fictional/ideal assumptions, not measurements. Display rounds to at most three decimals.

claims.text: A unit price expresses cost per stated quantity; comparable unit-price labels use consistent units of measure.
claims.source: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/1181e2025/NIST.SP.1181e2025.html NIST SP 1181-2025, Definitions / Unit Pricing and E-Commerce. Opened 2026-10-13. Dataset prices and package amounts are invented for the arithmetic demonstration.

recall.question: A costs €3 for 500g. B costs €6 for 900g. Change only Large-price to 7.5€. What is B (900g) now?
recall.why: Use B's stated rule with Large-price=7.5€: it gives 8.333€/kg. Dividing price by kilograms puts both packs on the same denominator. Pack size alone does not determine unit price; the receipt and quantity must travel together.

safety.assumptions: A costs €3 for 500g. B costs €6 for 900g.
safety.excluded: No chemical mixtures, medical advice, wiring, safety-device bypass, actual tariffs, financial recommendations, temperature, food-storage or food-safety instructions. All energy powers, durations and tariffs are illustrative.
